newsitem.title: USA: Conrail board meets, assets seen split.
newsitem.headline: Conrail board meets, assets seen split.

text.p: The four-month-old takeover battle for Conrail Inc. seemed to be nearing an end Monday as the company's board met amid signs its assets would be divided between rival bidders CSX Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp.

Although several options were reported to be under consideration, Wall Street sources speculated that the most likely outcome would be for CSX to match Norfolk Southern's offer of $115 a share, or about $10.3 billion. CSX then would turn around and sell half of Conrail's assets to Norfolk Southern.
The existing merger pact between Conrail and CSX is valued at $9.6 billion, or $108 a share.
The three railroads have been negotiating an end to the stalemate that occurred in January, when Conrail shareholders rejected a key measure needed for the CSX deal to proceed.
Norfolk Southern has repeatedly insisted that it would not accept any transaction that values Conrail at less than $115 a share.

Conrail said its board of directors would meet to weigh options regarding its proposed merger with CSX but declined to elaborate. Sources familiar with the situation said the board meeting began in the morning and continued into the afternoon.
It was not immediately clear whether CSX's board had authorised a higher bid for Conrail. CSX repeatedly has said it would not raise its offer.
CSX and Norfolk Southern declined to comment.

Wall Street welcomed the prospect of an end to the stalemate, bidding up the shares of all three companies. Conrail jumped $7.125 to $111.625, CSX rose $2.875 to $49 and Norfolk Southern gained $2.75 to $93.875, all in consolidated New York Stock Exchange trading.
Analysts had long speculated that a division of Conrail's assets would be the likely conclusion of the takeover fight.
"This may be the final chapter. All sides are coming out as winners," said Thomas Galvin of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
A division of Conrail's assets would enhance railroad competition in the Northeast, analysts said. Furthermore, they noted that dividing Conrail would ease the financial burden on both bidders.

"Although the deal could still collapse, on the surface it does make much sense for both shareholders and regulatory authorities, as well as for shippers," Anthony Hatch, of NatWest Securities Corp., wrote in a report.

Sources familiar with the situation told Reuters on Sunday that negotiations to end the three-way battle had gained momentum and it appeared that a negotiated deal would be struck. They said a likely deal would call for Conrail's assets to be split between CSX and Norfolk Southern.
The sources said that both CSX and Norfolk had come to realise that neither would succeed in winning Conrail alone.
Furthermore, the sources said, Conrail, which previously had opposed a division of its assets, now believed that such a scenario would be the most likely ultimate outcome.
